extracted.intended_audience: scholars, clergy, and rulers interested in political theology and the relation of civil and ecclesiastical authority
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of rules and principles relating to the proper relation between civil sovereign power and religious authority, grounded in Biblical precedents (Abraham, Moses, the High Priest, Kings) and Christ's offices. The chapter sets out who may lawfully interpret revelation, who may command external worship, and when obedience to magistrates is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sovereign as sole governor of State and Religion
rubrics_metrics.description: “Governour both of the State, and of the Religion... that Governor must be one; or else there must needs follow Faction, and Civil war in the Common-wealth, between the Church and State...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If pastors (or civil sovereigns) are not subordinate so as to yield one chief pastor, men will be taught contrary doctrines and faction will follow; therefore the sovereign should be the single chief pastor (i.e. ultimate authority) to avoid civil and religious division.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abrahamic covenant establishes patriarchal religious authority
rubrics_metrics.description: “The Covenant which Abraham made with God... was to take for the Commandement of God, that which in the name of God was commanded him, in a Dream, or Vision, and to deliver it to his family, and cause them to observe the same.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abraham alone received revelation and by covenant bound his seed; from this Biblical precedent the author concludes that a familial/sovereign head has lawful power to bind his people in external religion when God speaks to him.

rubrics_metrics.name: Positive commandments from sovereign when no direct revelation
rubrics_metrics.description: “They to whom God hath not spoken immediately, are to receive the positive commandements of God, from their Soveraign; as the family and seed of Abraham did from Abraham their Father, and Lord, and Civill Soveraign.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where subjects lack immediate supernatural revelation, they should accept as divine commands those positive religious obligations promulgated by their sovereign.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inward thought and belief exempt from sovereign law
rubrics_metrics.description: “As for the inward Thought, and beleef of men, which humane Governours can take no notice of... they are not voluntary... and consequently fall not under obligation.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sovereign authority pertains to external acts and profession of religion; inner belief remains solely known to God and is not enforceable by human rulers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punishment of private spirit opposing sovereign
rubrics_metrics.description: “it was not unlawfull for Abraham... for the countenancing of any doctrine which Abraham should forbid... to punish them; and consequently that it is lawfull now for the Soveraign to punish any man that shall oppose his Private Spirit against the Laws.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims of private revelation that seek to contravene the sovereign's established religion may legitimately be punished by the sovereign to maintain public order and uniform external worship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sovereign as sole interpreter of God's word
rubrics_metrics.description: “none but the Soveraign in a Christian Common-wealth, can take notice what is, or what is not the Word of God.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation of Scripture (i.e. determining what is properly God's command for the polity) belongs to the sovereign; individuals must not usurp the role of judging whether the sovereign governs according to God.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moses' authority grounded in public consent and signs
rubrics_metrics.description: Moses' authority depended on the opinion the people had of his sanctity and the verity of his miracles; the people promised obedience when they said to Moses, 'speak thou with us, and we will hear.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A leader's claim to speak for God before a people may be validated by miraculous signs and the people's consent; where that consent and sign are present, people are obliged to obey what the leader delivers as God's command.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moses as sole sovereign and representative under God
rubrics_metrics.description: “Moses... was their sole Soveraign under God... he onely went for the businesse of the people... And though afterwards it be said... yet this was not till after Moses had been with God before, and had brought to the people the words which God had said to him.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The person who alone receives and conveys God’s commands (Moses-figure) holds sole sovereign authority in both civil and religious matters during his tenure; others are not to approach or presume the same authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prophetic authority subordinate to sovereign's spirit
rubrics_metrics.description: “God came down in a cloud, and took of the Spirit that was upon Moses, and gave it to the Seventy Elders... the sense of the place is... that God endued them with a mind conformable, and subordinate to that of Moses.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prophets or those who prophesy derive and exercise their authority subordinately through the sovereign (or founder); extraordinary prophetic activity is legitimate only insofar as it is consistent with and authorized by that sovereign's doctrine.

rubrics_metrics.name: High Priest's combined civil and ecclesiastical sovereignty under the covenant
rubrics_metrics.description: After Moses, the kingdom as a sacerdotal kingdom descended to Aaron's heirs: 'the Supreme Power of making War and Peace, was in the Priest... The Supreme Power of Judicature belonged also to the High Priest.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under the covenantal constitution of Israel the High Priest (as successor in the sacerdotal kingdom) held both temporal and spiritual authority — governing war, peace, judicature, and worship — and persons in that office represented God's person on earth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right of religious supremacy accompanies civil sovereignty (kings)
rubrics_metrics.description: “from the first institution of Gods Kingdome, to the Captivity, the Supremacy of Religion, was in the same hand with that of the Civill Soveraignty; and the Priests office after the election of Saul, was not Magisteriall, but Ministeriall.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the people established kings, civil sovereignty and supremacy in external religion were joined in the king's person; the king had authority over religious offices and rites unless he voluntarily limited them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actual practice does not nullify rightful sovereign supremacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Although in practice kings and rulers were often checked by prophets and varied in behaviour, 'from the practise of those times, there can no argument be drawn, that the right of Supremacy in Religion was not in the Kings.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical abuses, revolts, or the people's changing allegiance do not erase the original right of the sovereign to exercise supremacy in religion; practice and right must be distinguished.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disruption (captivity) removes settled commonwealth but not the principle connecting sovereignty and worship
rubrics_metrics.description: During the Captivity and subsequent subjection to foreign powers the Jews had no settled commonwealth; nevertheless 'so far forth as concerneth the Old Testament... whosoever had the Soveraignty of the Common-wealth amongst the Jews, the same had also the Supreme Authority in matter of Gods externall worship.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even in periods of political disruption, the normative principle stands: whoever holds sovereign civil power also holds authority over the externals of worship when the polity is restored.

rubrics_metrics.name: Christ's threefold office: Redeemer, Prophet/Pastor, and King
rubrics_metrics.description: “We find in Holy Scripture three parts of the Office of the Messiah: the first of a Redeemer... The second of a Pastor, Counsellour, or Teacher... The third of a King, and Eternall King, but under his Father...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The offices correspond to different times and functions: redemption by sacrifice, conversion by preaching and ministry, and future kingship exercised after the final coming; each office has distinct scope and temporal application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Christ's earthly mission did not establish temporal kingship here and now
rubrics_metrics.description: “My Kingdome is not of this world... the Kingdome of Christ is not to begin till the general Resurrection.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While Christ is redeemer and teacher during his earthly ministry, he does not exercise the kingly office over the present temporal world; his kingship (in the full, governing sense) begins at the resurrection and last judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Christ's preaching does not negate obedience to existing magistrates
rubrics_metrics.description: Christ 'commanded to obey those that sate then in Moses chaire, and to pay tribute to Caesar' and 'I came not to judge the world, but to save the world.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The teaching and miracles of Christ were not seditious; Christians are enjoined to obey civil magistrates and not to use Christ's ministry as a warrant to overthrow lawful civil authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Christ's future kingship is subordinate to the Father and analogous to Moses' office
rubrics_metrics.description: Christ will reign as King 'under his Father' and in office resemble Moses: apostles shall 'sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel' when the Son of man shall come in the throne of his glory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Christ's kingship in the world to come is exercised in human nature under the Father’s superior authority and mirrors the mediated authority pattern (like Moses and his deputies): delegated judges (apostles) will share in that judicial rule.
